title: Jensen Huang Is Out. Everything in AI Is Now Up for Grabs.
dek: After a week of escalating revelations — a second affair, a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and Nvidia's intervention in a Commerce probe — Jensen Huang is out as Nvidia's CEO. Forget the who-did-it speculation for a moment: the bigger story is what changes when the AI industry's linchpin, China bridge, open-source champion and de facto financial backstop is suddenly gone.

oneIdea.headline: Jensen Huang wasn't just Nvidia's CEO. He was load-bearing for the whole AI industry, and now everything he held up is in play.
oneIdea.summary: Whether or not anyone coordinated his fall, Jensen Huang is gone, and the more useful question is what shifts now. He was the US's key bridge to China and TSMC, the loudest champion of open source, Anthropic's chief philosophical opponent in Washington, and the adult in the room backstopping financing for labs and neoclouds. Nvidia will probably find a bottom and stabilize, but its long-term destiny looks diminished. China hawks gain leverage, open source loses its best advocate, and the build-out may lose the closest thing it had to a Federal Reserve chair. Under all of it sits a growing, bipartisan sense that the biggest private companies have simply grown too powerful.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Limited clinical relevance; watch the supply chain
items.body: A change of chief executive at a chip maker does not alter anything in the consulting room. The indirect link is financing. NLW says Nvidia's guarantees held up smaller AI companies; Zitron says that support hid weak businesses. Either way, some suppliers of NHS tools rent their computing from firms that depended on it, so ask vendors where their service is hosted and what their continuity plan is.

items.title: Open models matter for data kept on site
items.body: NLW notes that open models have lost their most prominent advocate in Washington. For the NHS, open models are what make it possible to run a tool inside a trust's own systems, so patient data never leaves. If American policy turns against them, that option could narrow. It is worth following, though nothing has changed yet.

items.title: Governance, not genius
items.body: The episode turned on a board with no succession plan and a senior lawyer reportedly leaning on a regulator. The lesson is ordinary and applies to any organisation, a practice or an out-of-hours provider included: no individual should be beyond challenge, relationships with direct reports are a governance matter, and succession should be planned before it is needed.

the_other_side.source: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Megaspeed
the_other_side.text: Zitron, in a paid piece published the day after of which only the opening is free to read, says the press is treating Huang's fall as tabloid material and missing the larger matter: his allegation that Nvidia misled people about how and where it makes its money. He repeats a short seller's claim that more than a fifth of last fiscal year's revenue may have come through diverted sales to China, and points to two earlier SEC actions against Nvidia over its disclosures. Where Whittemore mourns a load-bearing figure, Zitron concludes "we can't trust a damn word" Huang or Nvidia says. These are his allegations.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether Huang was holding the AI industry up or propping it up. Both accept as fact that he is out, that Nvidia's general counsel reportedly intervened in a Commerce Department probe, and that Nvidia's guarantees and investments underpin labs and neoclouds. The empirical question is whether that support, and Nvidia's reported revenue, survive scrutiny under new management; the observable is Nvidia's next results and guidance under its interim chief executive, and whether it keeps backstopping customers. The residue is worldview: whether one man's judgement built an industry or disguised its weakness. For Whittemore to be vindicated, Nvidia must stabilise while the losses fall on China ties, open models and the pace of building. For Zitron, investigators must show material diverted revenue and the financing web must contract. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both think Nvidia's backstops are the thing most at risk. Watch Nvidia's results later this month.

headlines.headline: Jensen Huang is out as Nvidia's CEO, and off the board too
headlines.summary: Nvidia announced Thursday morning that Huang is leaving both the CEO role and his board seat. Former Synopsys CEO Harvey C. Jones becomes the company's first-ever chairman, and CFO Colette Kress adds the role of interim CEO until the board finds a permanent replacement.

headlines.headline: A second affair, this time with a direct report
headlines.summary: Citing five sources, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare, who reports to him directly. His security team allegedly pressured a bystander who filmed them at GTC to sign an NDA. The episode has none of the geopolitical intrigue of the first affair, but it turned what looked like a one-off slip into a pattern of poor judgment.

headlines.headline: The board went from "confidence" to ouster in four days
headlines.summary: On Sunday, Nvidia's board expressed "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team." Days of reporting followed noting the company had no succession plan, and the president called Huang "a very honorable guy." By Wednesday the board had convened an emergency meeting to remove him.

headlines.headline: The spark: a State Department memo about a Singaporean neocloud executive
headlines.summary: The Times obtained a State Department memo claiming that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at the Singaporean neocloud Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence agent who had grown close to Jensen. The Financial Times added that US intelligence believed the relationship was romantic. Jensen admitted infidelity but did not address the spy allegations.

headlines.headline: Nvidia's general counsel reportedly leaned on a Commerce investigation
headlines.summary: Reporting suggested Nvidia's general counsel intervened in the Commerce Department's investigation into Megaspeed, apparently name-dropping a senior Commerce official, after which the probe went away. Commerce staff called it, at minimum, a breach of procedure.

headlines.headline: Megaspeed was one of Nvidia's biggest Southeast Asian customers
headlines.summary: Commerce opened its Megaspeed investigation in late 2024 over allegations that the company was diverting physical chips into China, not just offering remote access. According to The Information, Megaspeed bought at least $7.5 billion in advanced AI chips after its 2023 founding.

headlines.headline: The debate was never really about the affair
headlines.summary: Early in the week, defenders made two arguments: an affair is a human failing, and Jensen is irreplaceable. The core question, though, was national security. As the week went on, more people concluded that losing Jensen would be a huge blow, but keeping him on could be worse.

headlines.headline: Jensen Huang is a brilliant man and a fool.
headlines.summary: The Economist's editorial argued that, like many powerful leaders, Huang came to believe he was too important for the normal rules to apply to him, and that his should not be the only head to roll.

headlines.headline: The potential for extortion is so tremendous with something as sensitive as Nvidia chips.
headlines.summary: Calls to resign came from both sides of the aisle. Cramer's conclusion: "I just think he's got to go."

headlines.headline: The board's bind, and a telling silence
headlines.summary: Axios's Dan Primack asked what else a board could do after confirming its CEO lied about one affair with national security implications while sleeping with a direct report. His read on the final announcement: "Zero comment from Jensen in the press release. That's very telling about how not voluntary this was."

headlines.headline: To many observers, the timing felt coordinated
headlines.summary: As the second story landed, a wide swath of tech and media voices began asking who benefits and why now. Replit's Amjad Masad suggested that anyone who wants AI "closed, centralized, and controlled" gains from removing open source's premier champion. Glenn Greenwald questioned whether there was any tangible evidence beyond anonymous intelligence suspicions.

headlines.headline: Is Jensen's fall a win for China or a loss?
headlines.summary: The sourcing has openly come from US intelligence. The harder question is whether China gains more from Nvidia funneling it chips or from disrupting a US company with 90% market share now that Huawei is catching up. China may have planned this over decades, or it may simply be a happy accident.

headlines.headline: The steelman for why Democrats might welcome this
headlines.summary: With anti-AI populism surging after the midterms, a high-profile Jensen scandal lets new leaders placate voters, tie the story to a Trump national security scandal, and schedule a year of hearings. It does all that without the truly disruptive moves: a data center moratorium, a ban on recursive self-improvement, or a breakup. NLW is explicit that this is a steelman, not his own view.

headlines.headline: Lutnick is cast as obstructer-in-chief on chip exports
headlines.summary: Axios reports that Treasury Secretary Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room over Commerce's failure to enforce export controls on Megaspeed. Trump called Elon Musk for advice, Musk sided with the hawks, and the president said "Let's get it done." Trump approved action on at least three occasions (May, August and November 5), and it still hasn't happened.

headlines.headline: The Occam's razor explanation: China hawks seizing their moment
headlines.summary: Chinese firms are reportedly rushing to rent capacity at Southeast Asian data centers before the remote-access loophole in export controls closes. The hawks aren't satisfied even with that fix, and this scandal gives them leverage to force through action they've never been able to get.

headlines.headline: The most speculative thread points at Anthropic
headlines.summary: A viral post argued that the Times reporter who broke the spy story had relied on Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark as a source in past AI coverage. The backdrop: Dario Amodei and Jensen famously don't get along and sit at opposite poles on AI risk, China policy and open source. NLW lays out the basics without endorsing the theory.

headlines.headline: Anyone inside AI who did this is playing with fire
headlines.summary: Publisher Sam Koppelman's reminder: Nvidia is anchoring the Anthropic IPO, investing in OpenAI, backstopping neoclouds like CoreWeave and guaranteeing Stargate data centers, all through deals Jensen negotiated personally. In an industry this interconnected, taking him out hurts everyone.

headlines.headline: The US just lost its key human bridge to China and TSMC
headlines.summary: Beyond the policies he pushed, Jensen personally connected US and Chinese political and business communities, and he was major connective tissue with TSMC in Taiwan. Losing him from those conversations matters regardless of what Nvidia's policy positions become.

headlines.headline: The architect of US chip leadership is out of play
headlines.summary: Jensen made early, contrarian bets that put Nvidia and the US in front. In the long run, reducing key-man risk could leave the sector healthier five or ten years out, as companies like AMD and Google benefit from a less dominant Nvidia.

headlines.headline: Open source just lost its biggest advocate in Washington
headlines.summary: Powerful forces in Washington see open source as a safety risk and an obstacle to control. Nvidia's Nemotron models were gaining enterprise traction, and even if Nvidia keeps building them, the uncertainty could slow corporate adoption of open models. Meta and Thinking Machines Lab gain ground as open-source leaders.

headlines.headline: Anthropic, x-risk advocates and China hawks all gain in Washington
headlines.summary: With its chief philosophical opponent neutered, Anthropic's influence in Washington likely grows. Sam Altman has historically sat between the two poles. Existential-risk advocates lose their strongest denier, and China hawks gain momentum for tighter export controls, which puts the screws on regions like the Gulf to choose sides.

headlines.headline: Nvidia likely finds a bottom, but its destiny looks diminished
headlines.summary: There is no greater capitulation than the CEO of the world's largest company resigning, so a near-term bottom and eventual stabilization, perhaps at a repriced level, seem likely. Jensen's real value, though, was the momentum behind long-term bets that replacement leadership rarely provides. As Naval put it, one does not simply replace the founder.

headlines.headline: The AI industry just lost its Federal Reserve chair
headlines.summary: Nvidia has been the adult in the room guaranteeing financing for smaller companies and model labs, the same web of backstops the AI bears worry about. New leadership will likely use this moment to reset expectations toward Wall Street's wishes rather than build out as fast as humanly possible. That is an underappreciated shift with implications that are hard to overstate.

headlines.headline: Everything coming out at once doesn't require a conspiracy
headlines.summary: Once a previously unimpeachable CEO falls, journalists hammer every source they have, and sources realize there will never be a more resonant moment to talk. The more that comes out, the more likely it is that more comes out. Don't assume we're done.

headlines.headline: The real story: a growing sense that big tech has too much power
headlines.summary: Pieces like The Atlantic's "The Scandal Is Bigger Than Jensen Huang" and a TikTok from journalist Jacob Ward are livid less about Jensen than about corporate power itself. Ward goes so far as to argue the public should have a democratic say in whether a CEO stays, which is far outside recent American norms. NLW expects this push, from both sides of the spectrum, to rebalance power toward government to grow in importance.
